newsitem.title: UK: Gold Outlook-Shock waves roll through industry.
newsitem.headline: Gold Outlook-Shock waves roll through industry.

text.p: Shock waves were still being felt in the gold markets on Monday after the bombshell from the Reserve Bank of Australia (RBA) late last week.
Gold prices fell to their lowest levels in 12 years -- around $324 per ounce -- after the RBA announce it had sold 167 tonnes of gold from its reserves over the past six months.

That cleaned about 60 percent of the RBA's gold out of the vaults and sent bearish messages to the market, especially as Australia is the world's third largest producer -- it mined 289 tonnes last year -- after South Africa and the U.S.
Bullion dealers expect investor selling to step up this week. The U.S. Independence Day holiday last Friday may have only postponed some of the unloading, they said.
"Expect an orgy of selling over the next few weeks," one dealer said.

According to calculations from stockbroker T. Hoare and Co's mining equities analyst Roger Chaplin, many gold miners in Australia and South Africa will be suffering at gold prices of $320 -- never mind what gold dealers see as the market's likely downside target of $287.25, which could be reached shortly.
He said the average total costs of mining gold were around $350, including head office, exploration, depreciation and financing charges.
In South Africa the cost would be about $334.00, he said.
He said forward sales hedging programmes would help the miners for now.
The average hedge price received during the first quarter of 1997 was "close to $400 per ounce," Chaplin said.
Nevertheless, of the world's top 11 North American mining companies, "five or six will be on the border at today's prices."
He added, "We won't see closures just yet because the forward sales (hedge) contracts are still at a decent price."
However, raising financing for new mines could be a problem given that the cash cost for a new mine would have to be under $220 an ounce to make it profitable, he said.
"A $250 cash-cost mine is now very marginal," Chaplin said.
New mine financing was also caught in the dilemma that the value of mine reserves had to be reduced.
Chaplin also noted the industry as a whole still had to cope with the psychological issues involved in central banks reviewing gold reserve management policy.
The central banks and other institutions hold about 35,000 tonnes of gold in reserves.
"They are shaken up by central bank selling or the threat of it. The banks have something like nine years supply of newly mined gold just sitting there," he said.
The reverberations from the RBA announcement were still loud and strident late last week and on Monday.
Australian gold miners pressed the World Gold Council (WGC) to make a statement condemning the action.
The WGC expressed its "deep concern" and said the RBA action seemed to be "motivated by narrow financial considerations."

It added in a statement, "For a leading gold producer to take unnecessary actions that prejudice the well being of a key sector of its economy suggests a lack of sensitivity to the factors impacting the market."
